title: Operating Systems
summary: The software that runs everything else: what an operating system does, how it juggles processes and memory, how files and the command line work, why updates and permissions keep you safe, how open-source Linux powers the world, and how AI is reshaping the operating systems of the future.
learn: What an operating system is and the jobs it does
How an operating system manages processes, multitasking and memory

How updates, user accounts and permissions keep a system secure
The difference between open-source and proprietary software, including Linux

intro: Every time you switch on a laptop, phone, games console or smart TV, an operating system wakes up and takes charge. It shares out the processor and memory, keeps your files organised, protects you from malware and gives you something to click or tap. In this topic you'll discover what an operating system really does, peek behind the scenes with Task Manager and the command line, learn why updates matter, explore open-source Linux, and look at how AI is being built into the operating systems of the future.

pages.title: What does an OS do?
pages.spec: Define an operating system, describe its main functions and give examples for different devices
pages.summary: An operating system (OS) is system software that manages a computer's hardware and software and provides a user interface. Its main jobs are managing the processor, memory, storage, devices and security. Different devices use different operating systems, from Windows and Android to tiny embedded systems.
pages.starter: What would happen if every app on your phone tried to use the screen, speaker and camera at the same time with no one in charge?
sc: I can define an operating system
I can describe the main functions of an operating system

b: An operating system (OS) is the software that manages everything else
Sits between the hardware and your apps
Apps ask the OS for memory, storage, the screen and the internet
Without an OS, every app would need to control the hardware itself
Process management: shares out the CPU between programs
Memory management: decides what's in RAM
File management: organises storage into files and folders
Device management (drivers), security and the user interface
Desktops and laptops: Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS

blocks.text: What is an operating system?

An **[[operating system]]** (OS) is the most important piece of **[[system software]]**: software that runs the computer itself rather than doing a task for the user. The OS sits between the hardware and the applications. When an app wants to save a file, play a sound or connect to Wi-Fi, it asks the OS, which controls the hardware for it.
When you switch on a computer, a small program in its firmware starts and loads the OS from storage into memory. This is called **[[booting]]**.
Functions of an operating system

head: Function
What it means
Example
rows: Shares the CPU between running programs
Music keeps playing while you type an essay
Decides which programs and data are in RAM
Moving an unused app out of RAM to make space
Organises data on storage into files and folders
Saving, renaming, moving and deleting files
Printing to a new printer after its driver installs
Controls who can log in and what they can access
Lets people interact with the computer

pages.title: Processes and memory
pages.spec: Explain how an operating system manages processes, multitasking and memory
pages.summary: A running program is a process. The CPU can only run a few things at once, so the OS switches between processes very quickly, making it look as if everything runs at the same time. The OS also manages RAM, using virtual memory on storage when RAM is full, which slows things down.
pages.starter: Open Task Manager (Ctrl + Shift + Esc). How many processes are running? Did you start them all?
sc: I can explain what a process is and how multitasking works
I can explain how the OS manages RAM and virtual memory
I can use Task Manager to investigate processes

b: A process is a program that is running
One app can have many processes (each browser tab may be one)
Background processes: updates, antivirus, syncing
Task Manager (Windows) and Activity Monitor (Mac) show them
A CPU core runs one thing at a time
The OS scheduler gives each process a tiny time slice, thousands of times a second
It looks like everything is running at once
Multi-core CPUs really can run several at once
RAM holds running programs and their data
The OS gives each process its own space, so they can't interfere
When RAM is full, virtual memory uses storage as overflow
Storage is much slower than RAM, so the computer slows down

blocks.text: Processes

A **[[process]]** is a program that is currently running. A single app can create several processes: modern web browsers often run each tab as a separate process, so one crashing tab doesn't bring down the whole browser. Many processes run in the background, such as antivirus scans, cloud syncing and update checks.
Multitasking and scheduling

**[[multitasking|Multitasking]]** means running more than one program at a time. Each CPU core can only carry out one instruction stream at a time, so the OS uses **[[scheduling]]**: it gives each process a tiny slice of CPU time, then switches to the next, thousands of times every second. This is so fast it looks as if everything is running at once. Multi-core CPUs can genuinely run several processes simultaneously, one per core.

blocks.title: Time slicing
blocks.context: Three processes need the CPU: Music, Browser and Antivirus. The scheduler gives each 10 milliseconds in turn.
steps: 0-10 ms: Music. 10-20 ms: Browser. 20-30 ms: Antivirus.
30-40 ms: Music again, and so on.
blocks.answer: Each process gets about 33 turns per second, so to you all three seem to run at the same time.

blocks.text: Memory management

**[[RAM]]** (random access memory) holds the programs and data currently in use. The OS decides how RAM is shared and keeps each process in its own separate area, so one program can't read or damage another's data.

When RAM fills up, the OS uses **[[virtual memory]]**: it moves data that isn't being used right now from RAM onto storage (SSD or hard drive) to make space. Storage is much slower than RAM, so a computer that relies heavily on virtual memory feels sluggish.
If your computer is slow, Task Manager's "Processes" tab shows which programs are using the most CPU and memory. Closing tabs and apps you aren't using frees RAM.

blocks.title: Task Manager investigation
steps: Open Task Manager (Ctrl + Shift + Esc) and choose "More details" if needed.
Record the CPU and memory use. Then open five browser tabs, a video and a document, and record again.
Find the three processes using the most memory.
Explain what you found using the words process, scheduling and RAM.

q.q: How did CPU and memory use change, and why?
q.a: Memory use rose because each new tab and app is a process that needs space in RAM; CPU use spiked while pages loaded and the video played, as the scheduler shared CPU time among more processes.

q.q: Why might a computer slow down when lots of apps are open?
q.a: RAM fills up, so the OS uses virtual memory on slower storage, and the CPU's time is shared between more processes.

o: A program that is currently running

check.q: How does a single CPU core multitask?
o: It runs everything at exactly the same time
The OS switches between processes very quickly
Storage used as overflow when RAM is full

check.q: Why does heavy use of virtual memory slow a computer down?
o: Storage is much slower than RAM

practice.q: Explain how an operating system allows several programs to appear to run at once on one CPU core.
practice.a: The scheduler gives each process a small time slice (1); switches between them very quickly (1); so fast they appear to run simultaneously (1).

practice.q: Explain why the OS keeps each process in its own area of memory.
practice.a: Stops one program reading/damaging another's data (1); improves security and stability/one crash doesn't affect others (1).

pages.title: Files and the command line
pages.spec: Describe how file systems organise data and use basic command-line instructions
pages.summary: The OS's file system organises storage into a hierarchy of folders (directories) and files, each with a path. File extensions show what type a file is. As well as a graphical interface, you can control a computer by typing commands in a command-line interface, a skill used widely by programmers and IT professionals.
pages.starter: Where is the last file you saved? Can you describe exactly how to get to it?
sc: I can describe how folders and files are organised in a hierarchy
I can write a file path and explain file extensions
I can use basic command-line instructions

b: The file system organises storage into folders (directories) and files
Folders inside folders make a hierarchy, like an upside-down tree
The top is the root (e.g. C:\ on Windows, / on Mac and Linux)
Each file has a path showing exactly where it is
Windows: C:\Users\Sam\Documents\Homework\essay.docx
Mac/Linux: /home/sam/Documents/Homework/essay.docx
The extension shows the file type: .docx, .pdf, .jpg, .mp4, .py, .exe
Be careful: .exe files run programs and can be malware
A command-line interface (CLI): type commands instead of clicking
Faster for some jobs; can automate repetitive tasks
Used by programmers, IT technicians and on servers with no screen
Windows: Command Prompt/PowerShell; Mac/Linux: Terminal

blocks.text: File systems

The **[[file system]]** is the part of the OS that organises data on storage. Data is stored in files, and files are organised into folders, also called **[[directory|directories]]**. Folders can contain other folders, forming a hierarchy that looks like an upside-down tree. The top level is the root.
Paths and extensions
A **[[file path]]** describes exactly where a file is, listing each folder from the root down.
A **[[file extension]]** is the part after the dot, showing what type of file it is and which program opens it.

Malware is often disguised with a double extension, like "homework.pdf.exe". Windows may hide the real extension, so it looks like a PDF but is actually a program. Turn on "show file extensions" in File Explorer.
The command line

A **[[command-line interface]]** (CLI) lets you control a computer by typing text commands. It's how computers were used before graphical interfaces, and it's still used by programmers, IT technicians and on servers that have no screen. It can be faster than clicking and lets you automate repetitive jobs with scripts.

blocks.caption: Basic commands
head: Task
Windows (Command Prompt)
Mac/Linux (Terminal)
rows: List files in the current folder

pages.title: Updates, accounts and security
pages.spec: Explain how operating system updates, user accounts, permissions and built-in security features protect a computer
pages.summary: OS updates fix bugs and security holes, so installing them quickly is vital; when an OS reaches end of support it stops getting fixes. User accounts and permissions control who can do what, and built-in tools such as antivirus, firewalls, sandboxing and app permissions add more layers of protection.
pages.starter: Your laptop says "Updates ready: restart now?" Do you click "Later"? Why might that be risky?
sc: I can explain why OS updates matter, including end of support
I can explain user accounts, administrator rights and permissions
I can describe built-in OS security features

b: Updates add features and fix bugs
Security patches fix vulnerabilities attackers could use
Once a fix is public, attackers race to use the hole on unpatched computers
Turn on automatic updates and restart when asked
Every OS version eventually stops getting updates
Windows 10 reached end of support in October 2025
Unsupported systems become more dangerous over time
Options: upgrade, pay for extended updates, or switch OS
Standard users can't change important system settings
Administrators can install software and change settings
Use a standard account day to day; admin only when needed
App permissions: camera, microphone, location, contacts

blocks.text: Updates and patches

A **[[vulnerability]]** is a weakness in software that an attacker could exploit. A **[[patch]]** is an update that fixes it. When a company releases a security patch, attackers study it to find the hole, then target computers that haven't installed the update. That's why delaying updates is risky.
End of support

Every OS version reaches **[[end of support]]**, after which the maker stops releasing security patches. Windows 10 reached end of support on 14 October 2025. Computers still running it no longer get free security updates unless they're enrolled in an extended (often paid) update scheme, so they become more vulnerable over time. Phones have the same problem: older models stop getting Android or iOS updates.

End of support creates a dilemma: many older computers can't run Windows 11, but replacing them creates e-waste. Some schools and charities give old laptops new life by installing a lightweight Linux OS or ChromeOS Flex.
Accounts and permissions

blocks.caption: Types of account
head: Account
Can do
Use it for
rows: Use apps, save own files, change own settings
Install software, change system settings, manage other users

blocks.text: **[[permissions|Permissions]]** control what each user or app is allowed to do. Using a standard account day to day means that if malware runs, it can't easily change the whole system. On phones, app permissions control access to the camera, microphone, location, contacts and photos.
Built-in security features

blocks.title: Layers of OS security
items: Antivirus, e.g. Microsoft Defender, scans for malware
**[[sandbox|Sandboxing]]**: apps run in a restricted area so they can't touch other apps' data (used on phones and in browsers)
Encryption of the whole drive (e.g. BitLocker, FileVault) protects data if a laptop is stolen
Secure sign-in: passwords, PINs, fingerprints, face recognition

blocks.title: Permission patrol
steps: Look at the list of 8 (fictional) apps and the permissions they request (e.g. a torch app wanting your contacts and location).
For each, decide which permissions are reasonable and which are suspicious.
Look at the update history of a school computer (screenshot) and identify any risks.
Write a 5-point security checklist for a new laptop.

q.q: Which app requests are suspicious, and why?
q.a: E.g. a torch app asking for contacts and location: a torch only needs the camera flash, so extra permissions suggest it's collecting data to sell or is malware.

q.q: Write your 5-point checklist for a new laptop.
q.a: Turn on automatic updates; use a standard account day to day; set a strong password or PIN plus Windows Hello; check antivirus and firewall are on; turn on drive encryption and back up files.

o: An update that fixes a bug or vulnerability

check.q: What does end of support mean?
o: The maker stops releasing security updates

check.q: Why use a standard account rather than administrator for everyday use?
o: Malware can't easily change the whole system
Running apps in a restricted area so they can't access other apps' data

practice.q: Explain why it's risky to delay installing security updates.
practice.a: Updates fix known vulnerabilities (1); once published, attackers know about the weaknesses (1); unpatched computers can be targeted/infected (1).

practice.q: Describe three built-in security features of a modern operating system.
practice.a: Any three: antivirus (1); firewall (1); sandboxing (1); drive encryption (1); user accounts/permissions (1); secure sign-in/biometrics (1); automatic updates (1).

pages.title: Open source and Linux
pages.spec: Compare open-source and proprietary software and describe the role of Linux
pages.summary: Proprietary software is owned by a company that keeps its code secret, while open-source software's code is public and can be studied, changed and shared. Linux is a free, open-source OS that runs most of the world's servers, all of the top supercomputers and, at its core, every Android phone.
pages.starter: Would you trust a recipe more if you could read every ingredient, or one that's kept secret? Does the same apply to software?
sc: I can explain the difference between open-source and proprietary software
I can describe where Linux is used and why
I can evaluate which type of software suits a situation

b: Source code: the human-readable instructions programmers write
Proprietary: owned by a company; code kept secret (Windows, macOS, iOS)
Open source: code is public; anyone can study, change and share it
Open source isn't always free, and free isn't always open source
Created by Linus Torvalds in 1991 as a student project
Runs most web servers and cloud computers
Runs all of the world's top 500 supercomputers
Android is built on the Linux kernel; so are many routers, TVs and cars
Open source: free, flexible, transparent, huge community
But support can be harder to find, and some software doesn't run on it
Proprietary: polished, official support, wide compatibility
But costs money and you can't see or change the code

blocks.text: Source code and licences
**[[source code|Source code]]** is the human-readable code that programmers write. A **[[licence]]** is a legal agreement setting out how software can be used, copied and changed.

blocks.caption: Open source vs proprietary
head: Feature
**[[open source|Open-source]]** software
**[[proprietary software|Proprietary]]** software
rows: Usually paid (or paid for by adverts or data)
Windows, macOS, iOS, Microsoft Office, Photoshop

blocks.text: Linux

**[[Linux]]** is a free, open-source operating system first created by Finnish student Linus Torvalds in 1991. Thousands of people and companies around the world now contribute to it. Linux comes in many versions called distributions (distros), such as Ubuntu, Fedora and Raspberry Pi OS.

blocks.title: Where Linux runs
items: Most of the world's web servers and cloud computers
All of the world's top 500 supercomputers
Android phones (built on the Linux kernel, the core of the OS)
Raspberry Pi computers, smart TVs, routers, cars and the International Space Station's laptops

blocks.text: Why choose open source?

Supporters say open source is more transparent (anyone can check the code for security problems), cheaper, and can be adapted to any need. Critics point out that some popular software and games don't run on it, it can be harder for beginners, and support relies on communities. Many organisations use a mix of both.

blocks.title: Choose the software
steps: Read the four scenarios: a charity reviving 50 old laptops; a hospital needing official support; a games streamer; a start-up building a website on cloud servers.
For each, decide whether to use open-source or proprietary software (or both) and choose an OS.
Justify each choice with at least two reasons.
Try a Linux distro if available (on a Raspberry Pi or in a browser-based Linux demo) and compare it with Windows.

q.q: What would you choose for the charity, and why?
q.a: A lightweight open-source Linux distro: it's free, runs well on old hardware, still gets security updates, and reduces e-waste.

q.q: What would you choose for the hospital, and why?
q.a: Probably proprietary software with official support (or a supported commercial Linux): medical systems need guaranteed support, certified compatibility and clear accountability.

o: Software whose source code is public and can be changed and shared

check.q: Which phone OS is built on the Linux kernel?

practice.q: Explain the difference between open-source and proprietary software.
practice.a: Open source: code is public and can be studied/changed/shared (1); proprietary: owned by a company, code secret, can't be changed (1).

practice.q: A charity wants to reuse 50 old laptops that can't run Windows 11. Evaluate whether it should install Linux.
practice.a: For: free, runs on older hardware, security updates, reduces e-waste (1-2); against: unfamiliar to users, some software won't run, support (1-2); conclusion (1). Max 4.

pages.title: The future of operating systems
pages.spec: Describe how operating systems are changing with on-device AI, the cloud and new kinds of devices, and evaluate the impacts
pages.summary: Operating systems are being reshaped by AI: new computers and phones have NPUs (neural processing units) so AI features run on the device, and OSs are adding AI assistants that can act across apps. Browser-based and cloud OSs, and OSs for headsets, cars and IoT, are growing. These changes raise questions about privacy, control and choice.
pages.starter: Imagine telling your laptop "Find the photo of my dog from last summer and send it to Gran" and it just does it. What would the OS need to be able to do?
sc: I can describe how AI is being built into operating systems
I can describe cloud-based and new-device operating systems
I can evaluate the benefits and risks of AI-powered operating systems

b: New chips include an NPU (neural processing unit) for AI tasks
On-device AI: features run locally, not in the cloud
Search your files by describing them; live captions and translation
AI assistants built into Windows, macOS, iOS and Android
AI agents can carry out multi-step tasks across apps for you
"Book the cheapest train and add it to my calendar"
The OS must manage what the AI is allowed to see and do
Permissions and human approval become even more important
Cloud-based OSs: ChromeOS runs mostly in the browser
Headset OSs for mixed reality, e.g. visionOS and Android XR
Car OSs that update over the air
Tiny OSs for billions of IoT devices

blocks.text: AI built into the OS

Many new laptops and phones contain an **[[NPU]]** (neural processing unit), a chip designed to run AI tasks efficiently. This allows **[[on-device AI]]**: AI features that run on the device itself rather than sending data to the cloud. On-device AI can be faster, work offline and keep personal data more private.

blocks.title: AI features in modern operating systems
items: Searching files and photos by describing them ("receipt from the bike shop")
Live captions and real-time translation of any audio
Writing tools that summarise, rewrite or proofread text in any app
Image editing, such as removing objects from photos
Voice assistants that understand natural requests

blocks.text: From assistants to agents

The next step is the **[[AI agent]]**: AI that can carry out multi-step tasks across apps on your behalf, such as finding information, filling in forms and booking things. For this to be safe, the OS needs to manage exactly what the AI can see and do, and ask the user to approve important actions.

blocks.caption: Weighing up AI in the OS
head: Benefits
Concerns
rows: Privacy: the AI may "see" everything on your screen
Accessibility: helps people with disabilities use computers
Security: attackers could trick an AI agent into doing harmful things
On-device processing can keep data private
Mistakes: AI can misunderstand or get things wrong
Natural language makes computers easier to use
Control and choice: AI features switched on by default; dependence on big companies

blocks.text: When Microsoft announced a feature that would take regular screenshots of a user's activity so they could search their history with AI, privacy experts raised serious concerns. Microsoft delayed it and changed it so it was off by default, encrypted and required sign-in to view. It shows how OS makers have to balance helpful features with privacy.
New kinds of operating system

items: **[[cloud-based OS|Cloud-based OSs]]** such as ChromeOS run most apps in the browser and store files online, so devices can be cheap and easy to manage, as many schools have found.
Mixed reality headsets have their own OSs (e.g. Apple's visionOS and Android XR) where apps float in your room.
Cars run complex OSs that receive updates over the air, like a phone.
Billions of IoT devices run tiny, efficient OSs that must be secure for years.

Automatic: organise files, suggest spelling fixes. Needs approval: sending messages, submitting work, buying anything. Never: share personal data with third parties, turn on the camera without the user's knowledge, delete files without confirmation.
